subject: biology
overview: Human Physiology covers how the body breathes, circulates blood, excretes wastes, moves, and coordinates its activities through nerves and hormones. It is one of the highest-weightage units in NEET Biology. Questions are mostly direct recall of NCERT facts such as numbers, names, sequences and functions, along with match-the-column and multi-statement items built on NCERT lines.

topics.explanation: Respiratory organs vary with habitat and level of organisation. Sponges, coelenterates and flatworms exchange $O_2$ and $CO_2$ by simple diffusion over the entire body surface. Earthworms use their moist cuticle and insects use a network of tracheal tubes. Most aquatic arthropods and molluscs use gills (branchial respiration). Fishes use gills, amphibians use moist skin (cutaneous respiration) as well as lungs, and reptiles, birds and mammals use lungs (pulmonary respiration). In humans the air pathway runs: external nostrils, nasal chamber, pharynx, larynx (cartilaginous sound box), trachea, primary bronchi, secondary and tertiary bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles and finally the thin, vascularised alveoli. The part from the nostrils to the terminal bronchioles is the conducting part. The alveoli and their ducts form the respiratory or exchange part. The lungs lie in an air-tight thoracic chamber and are covered by a double-layered pleura containing pleural fluid, which reduces friction.
key_points: Pharynx is the common passage for food and air
Epiglottis, a cartilaginous flap, covers the glottis during swallowing
Trachea divides into right and left primary bronchi at the level of the 5th thoracic vertebra
Trachea, primary, secondary and tertiary bronchi and initial bronchioles are supported by incomplete cartilaginous rings
Thoracic chamber is formed by the vertebral column dorsally, the sternum ventrally, the ribs laterally and the dome-shaped diaphragm below
Conducting part: filters, humidifies and brings air to body temperature
Steps of respiration: breathing, alveolar diffusion, transport by blood, tissue diffusion and cellular respiration
topics.neet_tip: Expect matching of animals to respiratory structures, such as sponges with body-surface diffusion and insects with tracheae, and questions on the sequence of the human air passage.
topics.topic: Breathing: respiratory organs and the human respiratory system

topics.explanation: Breathing consists of inspiration and expiration, driven by a pressure gradient between the lungs and the atmosphere. In inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and enlarges the thorax in the antero-posterior axis. At the same time the external intercostal muscles contract, lifting the ribs and sternum and enlarging the thorax in the dorso-ventral axis. Pulmonary volume increases, intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric pressure and air rushes in. Normal expiration is passive. The diaphragm and intercostals relax, thoracic and pulmonary volumes fall, intra-pulmonary pressure rises above atmospheric pressure and air is expelled. Abdominal muscles can increase the force of breathing. A healthy human breathes 12 to 16 times per minute. Regulation depends on several centres and receptors. The respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla sets the rhythm. The pneumotaxic centre in the pons moderates it by shortening inspiration and altering the rate. A chemosensitive area beside the rhythm centre is highly sensitive to $CO_2$ and $H^+$. Receptors in the aortic arch and carotid artery also detect these changes. Oxygen has an insignificant role in regulation.
key_points: Inspiration is active and involves contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles
Normal expiration is passive, through relaxation of the same muscles
Inspiration occurs when intra-pulmonary pressure is below atmospheric pressure
Expiration occurs when intra-pulmonary pressure is above atmospheric pressure
Spirometer is used to measure respiratory volumes
Respiratory rhythm centre is in the medulla oblongata
Pneumotaxic centre is in the pons
Increased $CO_2$ and $H^+$ raise the rate and depth of breathing

formulas.meaning: Minute ventilation: the volume of air a healthy person inspires or expires per minute

topics.neet_tip: NEET asks which muscles contract in inspiration, the location of the rhythm and pneumotaxic centres, and which chemical (CO2 or H+, not O2) drives regulation.
topics.topic: Mechanism of breathing and its regulation

topics.explanation: Alveoli are the primary site of gas exchange; exchange also occurs between blood and tissues. Both take place by simple diffusion along partial pressure gradients. Diffusion depends on the pressure gradient, the solubility of the gas and the thickness of the membrane. $CO_2$ is 20 to 25 times more soluble than $O_2$. The diffusion membrane has three layers: alveolar squamous epithelium, capillary endothelium and the basement substance between them. Its total thickness is much less than a millimetre. About 97% of $O_2$ is carried by RBCs as oxyhaemoglobin and about 3% is dissolved in plasma. Each haemoglobin molecule binds up to four $O_2$ molecules, which gives a sigmoid oxygen dissociation curve. High $pO_2$, low $pCO_2$, low $H^+$ and lower temperature (conditions in the alveoli) favour oxyhaemoglobin formation, while the reverse conditions in tissues favour dissociation. $CO_2$ is transported about 20 to 25% as carbamino-haemoglobin, about 70% as bicarbonate (formed with the help of carbonic anhydrase) and about 7% dissolved in plasma.
key_points: Atmospheric air: $pO_2$ 159 and $pCO_2$ 0.3 mm Hg
Alveoli: $pO_2$ 104 and $pCO_2$ 40 mm Hg
Deoxygenated blood: $pO_2$ 40 and $pCO_2$ 45 mm Hg
Oxygenated blood: $pO_2$ 95 and $pCO_2$ 40 mm Hg
Tissues: $pO_2$ 40 and $pCO_2$ 45 mm Hg
Every 100 mL of oxygenated blood delivers about 5 mL of $O_2$ to tissues
Every 100 mL of deoxygenated blood delivers about 4 mL of $CO_2$ to the alveoli
Tidal volume (TV) is about 500 mL
Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV) is 2500 to 3000 mL
Expiratory reserve volume (ERV) is 1000 to 1100 mL
Residual volume (RV) is 1100 to 1200 mL and can never be expelled, even by forcible expiration

formulas.meaning: Inspiratory capacity: total air inspired after a normal expiration
Expiratory capacity: total air expired after a normal inspiration
Functional residual capacity: air left in the lungs after a normal expiration
Vital capacity: maximum air breathed out after a forced inspiration
Total lung capacity: total air in the lungs after a forced inspiration
Reaction catalysed by carbonic anhydrase; runs forward at tissues and in reverse at alveoli

topics.neet_tip: Numerical questions on capacities, such as VC or FRC from given volumes, and the percentages of O2 and CO2 transport modes are frequent.
topics.topic: Exchange and transport of gases; respiratory volumes

topics.explanation: Asthma is difficulty in breathing that causes wheezing. It results from inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles. Emphysema is a chronic disorder in which the alveolar walls are damaged, so the respiratory surface area decreases; cigarette smoking is a major cause. Occupational respiratory disorders arise in industries involving grinding or stone-breaking, which produce so much dust that the body's defence mechanisms cannot cope. Long exposure causes inflammation that leads to fibrosis (proliferation of fibrous tissue) and serious lung damage. Workers in such industries should wear protective masks. Common examples are silicosis from silica dust and asbestosis from asbestos fibres.
key_points: Asthma: inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles, causing wheezing
Emphysema: damaged alveolar walls and reduced respiratory surface
Major cause of emphysema is smoking
Occupational disorders: dust inhalation leads to inflammation and then fibrosis
Prevention of occupational disorders: protective masks
topics.neet_tip: Usually tested through matching a disorder to its cause or symptom, for example emphysema with alveolar wall damage.
topics.topic: Respiratory disorders: asthma, emphysema, occupational disorders

topics.explanation: Blood is a special fluid connective tissue made of plasma (about 55%) and formed elements (about 45%). Plasma is 90 to 92% water and 6 to 8% proteins. The main plasma proteins are fibrinogen (clotting), globulins (defence) and albumins (osmotic balance). Plasma without clotting factors is called serum. RBCs are the most abundant cells. They are biconcave and lack a nucleus in most mammals. They are formed in red bone marrow, live about 120 days and are destroyed in the spleen. WBCs are nucleated and are of two kinds: granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) and agranulocytes (lymphocytes, monocytes). Platelets are cell fragments of megakaryocytes. ABO blood groups depend on the A and B antigens on RBCs and the antibodies in plasma. The Rh antigen is present in about 80% of humans. Coagulation is a cascade. Injury activates platelets and plasma factors to form thrombokinase, which converts prothrombin into thrombin. Thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads that trap formed elements to form a clot. $Ca^{2+}$ ions are essential for clotting.
key_points: RBC count: 5 to 5.5 million per $mm^3$
Haemoglobin: 12 to 16 g per 100 mL of blood
WBC count: 6000 to 8000 per $mm^3$
Platelet count: 1.5 to 3.5 lakh per $mm^3$
Neutrophils make up 60 to 65% of WBCs and are phagocytic
Eosinophils make up 2 to 3% and are linked to allergy
Basophils make up 0.5 to 1% and secrete histamine, serotonin and heparin
Lymphocytes make up 20 to 25% (B and T cells, immunity)
Monocytes make up 6 to 8% and are phagocytic
Group A has antigen A and anti-B antibody
Group B has antigen B and anti-A antibody
Group AB has both antigens and no antibodies; it is the universal recipient
Group O has no antigens and both antibodies; it is the universal donor
Erythroblastosis foetalis can occur in the second pregnancy of an Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive foetus
It is prevented by giving anti-Rh antibodies to the mother immediately after the first delivery

formulas.meaning: First key step of the clotting cascade
Soluble plasma protein converted into insoluble clot threads

topics.neet_tip: Watch for reversed statements such as 'fibrinogen is produced from fibrin', and for questions on the most and least abundant WBC and on the donor/recipient logic of blood groups.
topics.topic: Blood composition, blood groups and coagulation

topics.explanation: As blood passes through capillaries, some water and small water-soluble substances move out into the spaces between cells. Larger proteins and most formed elements stay in the vessels. This fluid is called interstitial or tissue fluid, and its mineral distribution is similar to that of plasma. Nutrients and gases are exchanged between blood and cells through this fluid. An elaborate network of lymphatic vessels collects the fluid, now called lymph, and drains it back into the major veins. Lymph is a colourless fluid containing specialised lymphocytes, which are responsible for immune responses. Lymph is also an important carrier of nutrients and hormones. Fats are absorbed through lymph in the lacteals present in the intestinal villi.
key_points: Lymph is colourless because it lacks RBCs
Lymph contains lymphocytes, which provide immunity
Lymph has fewer proteins than plasma
Lymph returns tissue fluid to the major veins
Lacteals in intestinal villi absorb fats into lymph
Lymph carries nutrients and hormones
topics.neet_tip: Asked as statements comparing lymph with plasma (no RBCs, fewer proteins, has lymphocytes) and on the role of lacteals in fat absorption.
topics.topic: Lymph: composition and function

topics.explanation: The human heart is mesodermal in origin. It lies in the thoracic cavity between the two lungs, slightly tilted to the left, and is about the size of a clenched fist. It is enclosed in a double-walled membranous pericardium containing pericardial fluid. It has four chambers: two thin-walled atria and two thick-walled ventricles. A thin muscular interatrial septum separates the atria, and a thick interventricular septum separates the ventricles. The tricuspid valve guards the opening between the right atrium and right ventricle. The bicuspid (mitral) valve guards the opening between the left atrium and left ventricle. Semilunar valves guard the exits into the pulmonary artery and the aorta. Nodal tissue conducts the heart's impulses: the SA node lies in the right upper corner of the right atrium, and the AV node lies in the lower left corner of the right atrium near the AV septum. The AV bundle (bundle of His) divides into right and left bundles that give rise to Purkinje fibres. The SA node is the pacemaker. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins return it, and capillaries allow exchange.
key_points: Fishes have a 2-chambered heart
Amphibians and most reptiles have a 3-chambered heart
Crocodiles, birds and mammals have a 4-chambered heart
Open circulation occurs in arthropods and molluscs
Closed circulation occurs in annelids and chordates
Atrioventricular septum is made of thick fibrous tissue
Valves allow one-way flow of blood
SA node generates 70 to 75 action potentials per minute
Artery and vein walls have three layers: tunica intima, tunica media and tunica externa
Veins have valves and thinner walls than arteries
Capillary walls are one cell thick (endothelium only)
Pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood; pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood
topics.neet_tip: Valve positions, the location of the SA and AV nodes, the SA node rate (70-75 per min) and the pericardium enclosing the heart are favourite one-liners.
topics.topic: Human heart and blood vessels

topics.explanation: The cardiac cycle is the sequence of events in one heartbeat. It begins with joint diastole, when all chambers are relaxed. The tricuspid and bicuspid valves are open and blood flows from the pulmonary veins and venae cavae into the ventricles through the atria, while the semilunar valves stay closed. The SA node then fires and causes atrial systole, which increases flow into the ventricles by about 30%. The impulse passes through the AV node and AV bundle to cause ventricular systole. The AV valves close, producing the first heart sound 'lub', and rising pressure opens the semilunar valves so blood enters the aorta and pulmonary artery. The ventricles then relax. The semilunar valves close, producing the second heart sound 'dub', and the AV valves reopen as ventricular pressure falls. One cycle lasts 0.8 s at 72 beats per minute. Each ventricle pumps about 70 mL per beat (stroke volume), giving a cardiac output of about 5 L per minute. The ECG records the electrical activity of the heart: the P wave, QRS complex and T wave.
key_points: P wave: atrial depolarisation, leading to atrial contraction
QRS complex: ventricular depolarisation, initiating ventricular systole
T wave: ventricular repolarisation; the end of T marks the end of systole
Counting QRS complexes over a given time gives the heart rate
First heart sound 'lub' is caused by AV valve closure
Second heart sound 'dub' is caused by semilunar valve closure
Athletes have a higher cardiac output than non-athletes

formulas.meaning: Cardiac output: volume pumped by each ventricle per minute
Duration of one cardiac cycle at a heart rate of 72 per minute

topics.neet_tip: Expect ECG wave–event matching, the cause of the lub and dub sounds, and cardiac output calculations.
topics.topic: Cardiac cycle, cardiac output and ECG

topics.explanation: In double circulation, blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit. In pulmonary circulation, the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. In systemic circulation, the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta, then through arteries, arterioles and capillaries to the tissues. Deoxygenated blood returns through veins and the venae cavae to the right atrium. The hepatic portal system carries blood from the intestine to the liver through the hepatic portal vein before it enters systemic circulation. The coronary system supplies the cardiac musculature. Heart activity is auto-regulated by nodal tissue, so the heart is myogenic. A cardiac centre in the medulla oblongata can moderate this activity through the autonomic nervous system. Sympathetic nerves increase heart rate, the strength of ventricular contraction and cardiac output. Parasympathetic nerves decrease heart rate, the speed of conduction and cardiac output. Adrenal medullary hormones also increase cardiac output.
key_points: Pulmonary circuit: right ventricle to lungs to left atrium
Systemic circuit: left ventricle to body to right atrium
Hepatic portal vein carries blood from the intestine to the liver
Coronary vessels supply the heart muscle itself
Human heart is myogenic
Neural moderation of heart activity is by the medulla oblongata through the ANS
Sympathetic stimulation increases heart rate and output
Parasympathetic stimulation decreases heart rate and output
topics.neet_tip: Usually tested as the effect of sympathetic versus parasympathetic stimulation and as the correct sequence of pulmonary or systemic circulation.
topics.topic: Double circulation and regulation of cardiac activity

topics.explanation: Normal blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg (systolic/diastolic). Repeated readings of 140/90 mm Hg or higher indicate hypertension, which leads to heart disease and also affects vital organs such as the brain and kidney. Coronary artery disease, also called atherosclerosis, affects the vessels that supply the heart muscle. Deposits of calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue narrow the lumen of these vessels. Angina pectoris is acute chest pain that occurs when not enough oxygen reaches the heart muscle. It can occur at any age in men and women but is more common in the middle-aged and elderly. Heart failure is the state in which the heart cannot pump blood effectively enough to meet the body's needs. It is also called congestive heart failure because congestion of the lungs is a main symptom. Heart failure differs from cardiac arrest, where the heart stops beating, and from a heart attack, where heart muscle is suddenly damaged by an inadequate blood supply.
key_points: Hypertension: blood pressure of 140/90 or above
CAD deposits: calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue
Angina: chest pain due to insufficient $O_2$ reaching the heart muscle
Heart failure: congestion of the lungs is the main symptom
Cardiac arrest is not the same as heart attack or heart failure

formulas.meaning: Systolic over diastolic pressure; 140/90 or above indicates hypertension

topics.neet_tip: Matching each disorder to its definition, and distinguishing heart failure from cardiac arrest and heart attack, is a common angle.
topics.topic: Circulatory disorders: hypertension, coronary artery disease, angina pectoris, heart failure

topics.explanation: Animals excrete nitrogen in three main forms, depending on water availability. Ammonia is the most toxic form and needs the most water for elimination. Ammonotelic animals include many bony fishes, aquatic amphibians and aquatic insects. They excrete ammonia as $NH_4^+$ ions by diffusion across body surfaces or fish gills, and the kidneys play no significant role. Terrestrial animals convert ammonia in the liver into less toxic urea, which needs less water. Ureotelic animals include mammals, many terrestrial amphibians and marine fishes, and some animals retain urea in the kidney matrix to maintain osmolarity. Uricotelic animals, such as reptiles, birds, land snails and insects, excrete uric acid as a pellet or paste with minimum water loss. Excretory structures also vary across animals. Protonephridia (flame cells) occur in flatworms, rotifers, some annelids and Amphioxus. Nephridia occur in earthworms, Malpighian tubules in insects, antennal or green glands in prawns and other crustaceans, and kidneys in vertebrates.
key_points: Toxicity and water needed: ammonia > urea > uric acid
Ammonotelic: bony fishes, aquatic amphibians, aquatic insects
Ureotelic: mammals, terrestrial amphibians, marine fishes
Uricotelic: reptiles, birds, land snails, insects
Protonephridia function mainly in osmoregulation
Cockroach excretes through Malpighian tubules

formulas.meaning: Simplified net conversion of ammonia to urea in the liver (ornithine cycle)

topics.neet_tip: Classic match-the-column: animal to excretory product, or animal to excretory structure.
topics.topic: Modes of excretion: ammonotelism, ureotelism and uricotelism

topics.explanation: The human excretory system consists of a pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra. The kidneys are bean-shaped and lie between the last thoracic and third lumbar vertebrae. Each kidney has an outer cortex and an inner medulla made of medullary pyramids, and it contains about one million nephrons. A nephron has a glomerulus and a renal tubule. The tubule runs from Bowman's capsule to the PCT, Henle's loop, the DCT and finally the collecting duct. Urine forms in three steps: glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption and tubular secretion. Filtration occurs through glomerular endothelium, basement membrane and podocytes of Bowman's capsule, and almost all blood constituents except proteins pass. The PCT reabsorbs nearly all nutrients and 70 to 80% of electrolytes and water. The descending limb of Henle's loop is permeable to water, while the ascending limb is impermeable to water but transports electrolytes. The collecting duct reabsorbs much water to concentrate urine. A counter-current mechanism involving Henle's loop and the vasa recta concentrates urine. Micturition begins when stretch receptors in the bladder wall signal the CNS.
key_points: Each kidney is 10 to 12 cm long, 5 to 7 cm wide, 2 to 3 cm thick and weighs 120 to 170 g
Hilum: the notch where the ureter, blood vessels and nerves enter or leave the kidney
Columns of Bertini: extensions of the cortex between the medullary pyramids
Malpighian body (renal corpuscle) = glomerulus + Bowman's capsule
Malpighian body, PCT and DCT lie in the cortex
Cortical nephrons have short loops, and their vasa recta is absent or highly reduced
Juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops dipping deep into the medulla
Medullary osmolarity gradient: 300 to 1200 mOsmol per L, maintained by NaCl and urea
Urine can become nearly four times as concentrated as the initial filtrate
PCT has simple cuboidal brush-border epithelium
PCT secretes $H^+$, $NH_3$ and $K^+$, helping maintain pH
DCT carries out conditional reabsorption of $Na^+$ and water, and reabsorbs $HCO_3^-$
Micturition: bladder smooth muscle contracts and the urethral sphincter relaxes
Daily urine output is 1 to 1.5 L, containing 25 to 30 g of urea
Urine is slightly acidic, with a pH of about 6
Glucose (glycosuria) or ketone bodies (ketonuria) in urine indicate diabetes mellitus

formulas.meaning: Normal glomerular filtration rate of a healthy individual
Percentage of filtrate reabsorbed by the renal tubules

topics.neet_tip: Statements on the permeability of the two limbs of Henle's loop, the functions of PCT and DCT, and numbers such as GFR and the osmolarity gradient are repeatedly tested.
topics.topic: Human excretory system and urine formation

topics.explanation: Kidney function is regulated by hormonal feedback involving the hypothalamus, the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) and, to some extent, the heart. Osmoreceptors respond to changes in blood volume, body fluid volume and ionic concentration. When excess fluid is lost, the hypothalamus triggers release of ADH (vasopressin) from the neurohypophysis. ADH increases water reabsorption from the later parts of the tubule, preventing diuresis. ADH also constricts blood vessels, which raises blood pressure and GFR. When GFR or blood pressure falls, JG cells release renin. Renin converts angiotensinogen into angiotensin I, which is further converted into angiotensin II. Angiotensin II is a powerful vasoconstrictor and raises glomerular blood pressure and GFR. It also stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone, which promotes reabsorption of $Na^+$ and water from distal tubule parts. This pathway is the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). Increased blood flow to the atria triggers release of atrial natriuretic factor (ANF), which causes vasodilation, lowers blood pressure and acts as a check on RAAS. Diabetes insipidus results from defective ADH synthesis or release and causes water loss and dehydration.
key_points: ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary
ADH promotes water reabsorption in the DCT and collecting duct
Increased body fluid volume switches off osmoreceptors and suppresses ADH release
JGA is a sensitive region formed where the DCT and afferent arteriole come in contact
Aldosterone causes $Na^+$ and water reabsorption
ANF opposes RAAS by causing vasodilation and lowering blood pressure
Diabetes insipidus produces large volumes of dilute urine

formulas.meaning: RAAS sequence triggered by a fall in GFR or blood pressure

topics.neet_tip: Expect sequence or statement questions on RAAS, the opposing roles of ANF and RAAS, and the cause of diabetes insipidus (ADH deficiency).
topics.topic: Osmoregulation and regulation of kidney function: renin-angiotensin, ANF, ADH, diabetes insipidus

topics.explanation: Besides the kidneys, several other organs help in excretion. The lungs remove large amounts of $CO_2$, about 200 mL per minute, along with significant quantities of water. The liver, the largest gland, secretes bile containing bilirubin, biliverdin, cholesterol, degraded steroid hormones, vitamins and drugs; most of these leave the body with digestive wastes. The skin has two types of glands with excretory roles. Sweat glands produce sweat, a watery fluid containing NaCl, small amounts of urea and lactic acid; the primary function of sweat is to cool the body. Sebaceous glands eliminate sterols, hydrocarbons and waxes through sebum, which also forms a protective oily covering on the skin. Small amounts of nitrogenous wastes are also eliminated through saliva.
key_points: Lungs remove about 200 mL of $CO_2$ per minute
Liver excretes bile pigments (bilirubin, biliverdin) and cholesterol
Sweat contains NaCl, urea and lactic acid
Sebum contains sterols, hydrocarbons and waxes
Saliva removes small amounts of nitrogenous waste
topics.neet_tip: Usually asked as matching an organ to the substance it excretes, such as sebaceous glands with sterols and waxes.
topics.topic: Role of other organs in excretion

topics.explanation: When the kidneys malfunction, urea accumulates in the blood, a condition called uremia. Uremia is highly harmful and may lead to kidney failure. In such patients urea is removed by haemodialysis. Blood is drained from a convenient artery, mixed with an anticoagulant such as heparin and pumped into a dialysing unit. The unit contains a coiled cellophane tube bathed in dialysing fluid that has the same composition as plasma except for nitrogenous wastes. Because of the concentration gradient, nitrogenous wastes diffuse out through the porous membrane. The cleared blood is mixed with anti-heparin and returned to the body through a vein. Kidney transplantation is the ultimate treatment for acute renal failure, and a donor who is a close relative is preferred to minimise immune rejection. Renal calculi are stones or insoluble masses of crystallised salts such as oxalates that form within the kidney. Glomerulonephritis is inflammation of the glomeruli of the kidney.
key_points: Uremia: excess urea in the blood
Heparin is the anticoagulant added before dialysis
Anti-heparin is added before blood is returned to the body
Dialysing fluid matches plasma minus nitrogenous wastes
Kidney transplantation is the ultimate treatment for acute renal failure
Renal calculi: kidney stones of crystallised salts such as oxalates
Glomerulonephritis: inflammation of the glomeruli
topics.neet_tip: Questions focus on the dialysis principle (diffusion along a concentration gradient) and on defining uremia, renal calculi and glomerulonephritis.
topics.topic: Excretory disorders, dialysis and artificial kidney

topics.explanation: Movement is a significant feature of living beings. Amoeboid movement occurs in macrophages and leucocytes by means of pseudopodia formed by streaming protoplasm, with microfilaments involved. Ciliary movement occurs in internal tubular organs lined by ciliated epithelium. Coordinated beating of cilia in the trachea removes inhaled dust and foreign particles, and cilia in the female reproductive tract help ova pass along it. Flagellar movement is whip-like beating of flagella. It drives swimming of spermatozoa, maintains the water current in the canal system of sponges and moves protists such as Euglena. Muscular movement is used for movement of the limbs, jaws and tongue. Muscle is mesodermal in origin and makes up about 40 to 50% of adult body weight. Muscles show excitability, contractility, extensibility and elasticity. Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary. Visceral (smooth) muscle is non-striated and involuntary and lines hollow visceral organs. Cardiac muscle is striated, branched and involuntary.
key_points: Sperm motility is due to flagellar movement
Ciliary movement clears the trachea and moves ova through the oviduct
Leucocytes and macrophages show amoeboid movement
Skeletal muscle: striated and voluntary
Visceral muscle: smooth and involuntary
Cardiac muscle: striated, branched and involuntary
Locomotion requires coordinated activity of the muscular, skeletal and neural systems
topics.neet_tip: Direct match questions link a cell or organ to its type of movement, for example sperm with flagellar movement or the trachea with ciliary movement.
topics.topic: Types of movement: ciliary, flagellar and muscular

topics.explanation: A skeletal muscle is made of fascicles, or muscle bundles, held together by connective tissue called fascia. Each muscle fibre is a syncytium enclosed by the sarcolemma, and its sarcoplasmic reticulum stores $Ca^{2+}$. Myofibrils show alternating light I bands, containing actin, and dark A bands, containing myosin. A Z line bisects each I band, and an M line lies in the middle of the A band. The sarcomere, the segment between two successive Z lines, is the functional unit of contraction. Contraction follows the sliding filament theory. A motor neuron releases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, generating an action potential that causes $Ca^{2+}$ release. $Ca^{2+}$ binds troponin and unmasks the myosin-binding sites on actin. Myosin heads, using energy from ATP hydrolysis, bind actin to form cross bridges and pull the thin filaments towards the centre of the A band. The sarcomere shortens: I bands narrow while A bands keep their length. Binding of fresh ATP breaks the cross bridge, and the cycle repeats until $Ca^{2+}$ is pumped back.
key_points: Each actin filament has two F-actin strands made of G-actin monomers
Tropomyosin runs along the actin filament
Troponin masks the myosin-binding sites on actin at rest
Each myosin monomer is a meromyosin with a head and short arm (HMM) and a tail (LMM)
Myosin head acts as an ATPase and has active sites for both ATP and actin
H zone: central part of the A band not overlapped by thin filaments
Motor unit: one motor neuron together with the muscle fibres it supplies
Muscle fatigue is due to lactic acid accumulation from anaerobic breakdown of glycogen
Red fibres: rich in myoglobin and mitochondria; aerobic
White fibres: less myoglobin and more sarcoplasmic reticulum; anaerobic

formulas.meaning: Energy for cross-bridge formation and the power stroke

topics.neet_tip: Expect questions on the role of Ca2+ and troponin, the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, and which bands shorten during contraction (I band and H zone, not A band).
topics.topic: Skeletal muscle: contractile proteins and muscle contraction

topics.explanation: The adult human skeleton has 206 bones and a few cartilages. The axial skeleton (80 bones) includes the skull, vertebral column, sternum and ribs. The skull has 22 bones (8 cranial and 14 facial), plus the U-shaped hyoid and three ear ossicles in each ear. It joins the vertebral column through two occipital condyles, making it dicondylic. The vertebral column has 26 vertebrae arranged from head to toe as 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 1 sacral (fused) and 1 coccygeal (fused). There are 12 pairs of bicephalic ribs: 7 pairs of true ribs, 3 pairs of vertebrochondral ribs and 2 pairs of floating ribs. The appendicular skeleton (126 bones) comprises the limbs and girdles, with 30 bones in each limb. Joints are of three types. Fibrous joints, such as the skull sutures, allow no movement. Cartilaginous joints, such as those between vertebrae, allow limited movement. Synovial joints have a fluid-filled cavity and allow considerable movement.
key_points: Forelimb: humerus, radius and ulna, carpals (8), metacarpals (5), phalanges (14)
Hindlimb: femur (the longest bone), patella, tibia and fibula, tarsals (7), metatarsals (5), phalanges (14)
Patella is the cup-shaped knee cap covering the knee ventrally
Pectoral girdle: clavicle and scapula
Glenoid cavity of the scapula forms the shoulder joint with the humerus
Pelvic girdle: two coxal bones, each formed by fusion of ilium, ischium and pubis
Acetabulum receives the femur
Pubic symphysis contains fibrous cartilage
First vertebra (atlas) articulates with the occipital condyles
Ball and socket joint: humerus with the pectoral girdle
Hinge joint: knee
Pivot joint: atlas and axis
Gliding joint: between carpals
Saddle joint: carpal and metacarpal of the thumb

formulas.meaning: Distribution of bones in the adult human skeleton
Cervical + thoracic + lumbar + sacral + coccygeal vertebrae

topics.neet_tip: Counting questions (vertebrae, ribs, limb bones), the head-to-toe order of vertebrae and the sequence of lower limb bones are frequently asked.
topics.topic: Skeletal system and joints

topics.explanation: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder affecting the neuromuscular junction. It causes fatigue, weakening and paralysis of skeletal muscle. Muscular dystrophy is progressive degeneration of skeletal muscle, mostly due to a genetic disorder. Tetany is rapid spasms, or wild contractions, of muscle caused by low $Ca^{2+}$ in body fluids. Arthritis is inflammation of the joints. Osteoporosis is an age-related disorder marked by decreased bone mass and an increased chance of fractures; decreased estrogen is a common cause. Gout is inflammation of the joints caused by accumulation of uric acid crystals.
key_points: Myasthenia gravis: autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction
Muscular dystrophy: genetic, progressive degeneration of muscle
Tetany: caused by low blood $Ca^{2+}$
Osteoporosis: reduced bone mass, linked to low estrogen
Gout: uric acid crystals deposited in joints
Arthritis: inflammation of joints
topics.neet_tip: Almost always a match-the-column of disorder and cause; remember that tetany means low (not high) Ca2+ and that myasthenia gravis is autoimmune.
topics.topic: Muscular and skeletal disorders: myasthenia gravis, tetany, muscular dystrophy, arthritis, osteoporosis, gout

topics.explanation: The neuron is the structural and functional unit of the neural system. It has three parts: a cell body, dendrites and an axon. The cell body contains cytoplasm with typical organelles and Nissl's granules. Dendrites are short, repeatedly branched fibres that also contain Nissl's granules and carry impulses towards the cell body. The axon is a long fibre whose branched end terminates in bulb-like synaptic knobs containing synaptic vesicles filled with neurotransmitters; it carries impulses away from the cell body. Neurons are classified by structure. Multipolar neurons, with one axon and two or more dendrites, occur in the cerebral cortex. Bipolar neurons, with one axon and one dendrite, occur in the retina. Unipolar neurons, with a cell body and one axon only, occur in the embryonic stage. Myelinated fibres are wrapped by Schwann cells forming a myelin sheath, with gaps called nodes of Ranvier; they occur in spinal and cranial nerves. Unmyelinated fibres are enclosed by Schwann cells without a myelin sheath and occur in autonomous and somatic neural systems. Nerves are bundles of such fibres.
key_points: Nissl's granules are present in the cell body and dendrites, absent from the axon
Dendrites carry impulses towards the cell body; axons carry them away
Multipolar neurons occur in the cerebral cortex
Bipolar neurons occur in the retina
Unipolar neurons occur in the embryonic stage
Schwann cells form the myelin sheath in the PNS
Nodes of Ranvier are gaps between adjacent myelin sheaths
topics.neet_tip: Neuron-type location matching (bipolar in the retina, multipolar in the cortex) and the presence or absence of Nissl's granules are typical items.
topics.topic: Neuron and nerves

topics.explanation: The human neural system has two divisions. The central neural system (CNS), made of the brain and spinal cord, is the site of information processing and control. The peripheral neural system (PNS) consists of all nerves associated with the CNS. Afferent fibres carry impulses from organs to the CNS, and efferent fibres carry impulses from the CNS to effectors. The PNS has a somatic division, supplying skeletal muscles, and an autonomic division, supplying involuntary organs and smooth muscles. The autonomic division is further divided into sympathetic and parasympathetic parts. The visceral nervous system comprises the nerves, fibres, ganglia and plexuses connecting the CNS with the viscera. The brain is protected by the skull and three cranial meninges: the outer dura mater, the very thin middle arachnoid and the inner pia mater. The forebrain consists of the cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus. The midbrain has the corpora quadrigemina and the cerebral aqueduct. The hindbrain consists of the pons, cerebellum and medulla. The midbrain, pons and medulla together form the brain stem.
key_points: Corpus callosum connects the two cerebral hemispheres
Cerebral cortex is grey matter; the inner tracts form white matter
Association areas handle intersensory associations, memory and communication
Thalamus is the major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling
Hypothalamus controls body temperature, eating and drinking, and secretes hormones
Limbic system (amygdala, hippocampus) controls sexual behaviour, emotions and motivation
Cerebellum is highly convoluted to accommodate more neurons
Medulla contains centres for respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretion
Pericardium surrounds the heart and is not part of the CNS
topics.neet_tip: Meninges order, the parts of each brain region, the functions of the hypothalamus, medulla and limbic system, and odd-one-out questions such as pericardium are common.
topics.topic: Human nervous system: central, peripheral and visceral

topics.explanation: Neurons are excitable because their membranes are polarised. At rest, the axonal membrane is more permeable to $K^+$, nearly impermeable to $Na^+$ and impermeable to the negatively charged proteins in the axoplasm. The axoplasm is high in $K^+$ and negative proteins and low in $Na^+$, while the outside fluid is the reverse. The sodium-potassium pump maintains these gradients by moving 3 $Na^+$ out for every 2 $K^+$ moved in. The outer surface is therefore positive and the inner surface negative; this potential difference is the resting potential. A stimulus makes the membrane freely permeable to $Na^+$, and rapid $Na^+$ influx reverses the polarity. This reversal is depolarisation, and the resulting action potential is the nerve impulse. Local currents depolarise the adjacent site, so the impulse travels along the axon. A rise in $K^+$ permeability then lets $K^+$ diffuse out, restoring the resting state (repolarisation). At synapses, transmission is either electrical (fast, rare) or chemical, where neurotransmitters cross the synaptic cleft and bind receptors on the post-synaptic membrane.
key_points: Resting state: outside positive, inside negative
Depolarisation is caused by $Na^+$ influx
Repolarisation is caused by $K^+$ efflux
Electrical synapse: membranes in very close contact; faster than chemical
Chemical synapse: synaptic cleft and neurotransmitters
Neurotransmitters open ion channels on the post-synaptic membrane
The new potential produced can be excitatory or inhibitory

formulas.meaning: Stoichiometry of the sodium-potassium pump that maintains the resting potential

topics.neet_tip: Statement questions test ion movements during depolarisation and repolarisation, the pump ratio, and differences between electrical and chemical synapses.
topics.topic: Generation and conduction of nerve impulse

topics.explanation: Hormones are non-nutrient chemicals produced in trace amounts that act as intercellular messengers, mostly from ductless endocrine glands. The hypothalamus secretes releasing hormones such as GnRH and inhibiting hormones such as somatostatin, which reach the anterior pituitary through the hypophysial portal system. The pituitary lies in the sella turcica and has two parts. The adenohypophysis consists of the pars distalis, which secretes GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH and FSH, and the pars intermedia, which secretes MSH. The neurohypophysis stores and releases oxytocin and vasopressin, both made in the hypothalamus. The pineal gland secretes melatonin, which regulates diurnal rhythms. The thyroid secretes $T_4$, $T_3$ and thyrocalcitonin. The parathyroids secrete PTH, which raises blood $Ca^{2+}$. The adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline and noradrenaline, the fight-or-flight hormones. The adrenal cortex secretes glucocorticoids such as cortisol and mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone. In the pancreatic islets, alpha cells secrete glucagon and beta cells secrete insulin. The testes secrete androgens, and the ovaries secrete estrogen and progesterone.
key_points: LH: stimulates androgen secretion in males; causes ovulation and maintains the corpus luteum in females
FSH: stimulates follicle growth in females; with androgens, regulates spermatogenesis in males
Oxytocin: contraction of the uterus during childbirth and milk ejection
Vasopressin (ADH): reabsorption of water and electrolytes in the kidney
Thyroid hormones regulate basal metabolic rate and support RBC formation
Thyrocalcitonin lowers blood $Ca^{2+}$
Adrenal cortex has three layers: zona glomerulosa (outer), fasciculata (middle) and reticularis (inner)
Cortisol: stimulates gluconeogenesis, is anti-inflammatory and suppresses immunity
Aldosterone: promotes $Na^+$ reabsorption and excretion of $K^+$ and phosphate
Glucagon is hyperglycemic and stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
Insulin is hypoglycemic and promotes glucose uptake and glycogenesis
Leydig cells secrete testosterone
Corpus luteum secretes progesterone, which supports pregnancy
topics.neet_tip: Heavily tested via match-the-column of hormone to source or action and multi-statements on pituitary parts and pancreatic cells.
topics.topic: Endocrine glands and hormones: hypothalamus, pituitary, pineal, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal, pancreas, gonads

topics.explanation: Hormones act by binding to specific receptor proteins present only in their target tissues. Each receptor is specific to one hormone, and binding forms a hormone-receptor complex. Receptors are of two kinds: membrane-bound and intracellular (mostly nuclear). By chemical nature, hormones fall into four groups. Peptide, polypeptide and protein hormones include insulin, glucagon and the pituitary and hypothalamic hormones. Steroids include cortisol, testosterone, estradiol and progesterone. Iodothyronines are the thyroid hormones, and amino-acid derivatives include epinephrine. Hormones that bind membrane receptors usually do not enter the cell. Instead they generate second messengers such as cAMP, $IP_3$ and $Ca^{2+}$, which regulate cellular metabolism. Steroid and thyroid hormones bind intracellular receptors and regulate gene expression or chromosome function. Hormones are also secreted by non-endocrine tissues. The GI tract secretes gastrin, secretin, CCK and GIP. The heart secretes ANF, and the kidney secretes erythropoietin. Hormone levels are commonly controlled by negative feedback.
key_points: Gastrin: stimulates secretion of HCl and pepsinogen
Secretin: stimulates release of water and bicarbonate from the exocrine pancreas
CCK: stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and bile release from the gall bladder
GIP: inhibits gastric secretion and motility
Erythropoietin from the JG cells of the kidney stimulates RBC formation
Steroid hormones are lipid-soluble and act on intracellular receptors
Protein hormones use second messengers
topics.neet_tip: Asked as which hormones use second messengers versus intracellular receptors, and through matching GI hormones to their actions.
topics.topic: Mechanism of hormone action; hormones as messengers and regulators

topics.explanation: Hyposecretion of GH in childhood causes stunted growth, called pituitary dwarfism; excess GH in childhood causes gigantism. Excess GH in adults, especially in middle age, causes acromegaly. Acromegaly produces severe disfigurement, especially of the face, often goes undetected for years and can lead to premature death. Hypothyroidism during pregnancy leads to cretinism in the baby, with stunted growth, mental retardation, low IQ, abnormal skin and deaf-mutism. In adult women, hypothyroidism causes irregular menstrual cycles. Iodine deficiency in the diet causes hypothyroidism and enlargement of the thyroid, called goitre. Exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease) is a form of hyperthyroidism. It causes thyroid enlargement, protruding eyeballs, increased BMR and weight loss. Diabetes mellitus involves prolonged hyperglycemia with loss of glucose in urine and formation of harmful ketone bodies, and it is treated with insulin therapy. Addison's disease results from underproduction of adrenal cortex hormones. It alters carbohydrate metabolism and causes acute weakness and fatigue.
key_points: Dwarfism: low GH in childhood
Gigantism: high GH in childhood
Acromegaly: high GH in adults
Cretinism: hypothyroidism in the developing baby
Simple goitre: iodine deficiency
Exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease): hyperthyroidism with bulging eyes
Diabetes mellitus: insulin deficiency or failure, with glycosuria and ketonuria
Addison's disease: adrenal cortex hypofunction
Diabetes insipidus is due to ADH deficiency and is not related to insulin
topics.neet_tip: Match disorder with hormone and gland, and distinguish acromegaly from gigantism by age of onset.
topics.topic: Hormonal disorders: dwarfism, acromegaly, cretinism, goitre, exophthalmic goitre, diabetes, Addison's disease

key_facts: Human vertebral column has 26 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 1 sacrum and 1 coccyx
Adult human skeleton has 206 bones: 80 axial and 126 appendicular
Each limb has 30 bones; the femur is the longest bone
Ribs: 7 pairs true, 3 pairs vertebrochondral (false), 2 pairs floating
Skull: 8 cranial + 14 facial bones; the full count with hyoid and 6 ear ossicles is 29
SA node generates 70 to 75 action potentials per minute; the cardiac cycle lasts 0.8 s
Stroke volume is about 70 mL; cardiac output is about 5 L per minute
Normal BP is 120/80 mm Hg; 140/90 or above is hypertension
Tidal volume is about 500 mL; residual volume is 1100 to 1200 mL; healthy breathing rate is 12 to 16 per minute
About 97% of $O_2$ is carried as oxyhaemoglobin
About 70% of $CO_2$ is carried as bicarbonate, 20 to 25% as carbamino-haemoglobin and 7% dissolved
$CO_2$ is 20 to 25 times more soluble than $O_2$
GFR is about 125 mL per minute (180 L per day); about 99% of filtrate is reabsorbed
Each kidney has about one million nephrons; medullary osmolarity rises from 300 to 1200 mOsmol per L
RBC count is 5 to 5.5 million per $mm^3$ and RBC lifespan is 120 days
WBC count is 6000 to 8000 per $mm^3$; neutrophils are the most abundant WBC and basophils the least
About 80% of humans are Rh positive
Sodium-potassium pump moves 3 $Na^+$ out for every 2 $K^+$ in
Pars intermedia secretes only MSH
Oxytocin and vasopressin are synthesised in the hypothalamus and released from the neurohypophysis
Pancreatic alpha cells secrete glucagon and beta cells secrete insulin
Pancreatic islets number 1 to 2 million and form 1 to 2% of pancreatic tissue
Cranial meninges from outer to inner: dura mater, arachnoid, pia mater
Sarcomere lies between two Z lines; the A band length stays constant during contraction
Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter at the neuromuscular junction
Pneumotaxic centre is in the pons; the respiratory rhythm centre is in the medulla
common_traps: Thinking fibrinogen is produced from fibrin: thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin, and serum is plasma without clotting factors.
Assuming the posterior pituitary synthesises oxytocin and ADH: it only stores and releases them, and they are made by hypothalamic neurosecretory cells.
Mixing up the limbs of Henle's loop: the descending limb is permeable to water but nearly impermeable to electrolytes, while the ascending limb is impermeable to water but transports electrolytes.
Believing the A band shortens during contraction: only the I band and H zone shorten, while the A band length is constant.
Treating pericardium as a brain covering: the meninges are dura mater, arachnoid and pia mater, and the pericardium surrounds the heart.
Assuming arteries always carry oxygenated blood: the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.
Linking tetany to excess calcium: tetany is due to low $Ca^{2+}$, and gout, not arthritis in general, is specifically due to uric acid crystals.
Confusing diabetes insipidus with diabetes mellitus: insipidus is ADH deficiency causing water loss, while mellitus is an insulin problem causing hyperglycemia.
quick_revision: Air path: nostrils, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli; trachea divides at T5
Inspiration is active (diaphragm and external intercostals contract); normal expiration is passive
$VC = IRV + TV + ERV$, $TLC = VC + RV$, $FRC = ERV + RV$
Clotting cascade: prothrombin to thrombin, then fibrinogen to fibrin, with $Ca^{2+}$ essential
ECG: P is atrial depolarisation, QRS is ventricular depolarisation, T is ventricular repolarisation
Lub is caused by AV valve closure; dub by semilunar valve closure
Valves: tricuspid between right atrium and right ventricle; bicuspid between left atrium and left ventricle
Toxicity order: ammonia > urea > uric acid; bony fish are ammonotelic, mammals ureotelic, birds uricotelic
RAAS raises BP; ANF lowers BP; ADH conserves water, and its deficiency causes diabetes insipidus
Contraction: ACh, action potential, $Ca^{2+}$ binds troponin, cross bridges form, sarcomere shortens
Vertebrae (26): 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 1 sacrum, 1 coccyx; lower limb sequence: femur, patella, tibia, tarsals
Hormonal disorders: GH excess in children causes gigantism, in adults acromegaly; iodine deficiency causes goitre; low adrenal cortex hormones cause Addison's disease
